unit.title: Contribute to and manage the change processes

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A government agency that issues trade licences must move its paper applications online within a year, as part of a national policy. What should the change manager make clear to officers first?
options: The names of the officers who may lose their posts
The exact software screens officers will use each day
The date of the party to mark the end of the change
Why the change is needed and what it means for their work

questions.stem: In Lewin's three-stage model of change, what happens in the "unfreeze" stage?
options: New ways of working are written into policy and routine
People are helped to see why the present way must change
The new system is installed and staff begin to use it
The change is reviewed a year after it has been finished

questions.stem: A municipal corporation brought in a new system to track purchase orders. Six months later, many officers have gone back to paper files. Which stage of Lewin's model was not completed?
options: Refreezing
Unfreezing
Moving
Forming

questions.stem: A manager lists the forces pushing for a change and the forces working against it, and gives each a score. Which tool is she using?
options: SWOT analysis
A Gantt chart
Force field analysis
Cost-benefit analysis

questions.stem: In a force field analysis for moving a records unit to a new building, the forces for the move score 4, 5 and 3, and the forces against score 3, 4 and 2. What is the difference between the two totals?
After a force field analysis, which approach usually works best to move a change forward?
options: Add as many new driving forces as possible, whatever the cost
Ignore the restraining forces, as the change is approved
Wait until the restraining forces disappear on their own
Weaken the strongest restraining forces and build support

questions.stem: In the ADKAR model of individual change, what do the five letters stand for?
options: Awareness, desire, knowledge, ability, reinforcement
Analysis, design, knowledge, action, review
Awareness, decision, kick-off, action, results
Assess, develop, keep, adjust, report

questions.stem: Officers at a ministry understand why a new case system is needed and want it to work, but nobody has shown them how to use it. Which ADKAR element is missing?
options: Awareness
Desire
Knowledge
Reinforcement

questions.stem: Two weeks after a restructuring was announced, many officers at an agency are angry and complain in the corridors. What does the change curve suggest the manager should do?
options: Treat the anger as misconduct and begin disciplinary action
Cancel the restructuring until the anger has passed
Ignore it, because the feelings will pass in a day or two
Accept it as a normal reaction, listen and give clear facts

questions.stem: Before changing how a municipal corporation collects property fees, the project lead plots each group by its power and its interest. Which groups need to be managed most closely?
options: Those with low power and low interest
Those with high power and high interest
Those with low power and high interest
Those with high power and low interest

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a change impact assessment?
options: To decide which officers should be promoted afterwards
To prove to the minister that the change will cost nothing
To find out who and what the change affects, and how much
To record the daily attendance of the project team

questions.stem: A readiness survey of 160 officers finds that 56 feel ready for a new appointment system. What percentage feel ready?
Which approach to telling staff in a public hospital's records department about a major change is best?
options: One detailed email from the director on the day it starts
Early, regular messages in several ways, with time for questions
Telling supervisors only, who decide what their staff should know
A notice on the board once every decision has been finalised

questions.stem: A ministry plans to change shift patterns for its customer service officers, who belong to a union. What should management do?
options: Bring in the new shifts and tell the union afterwards
Ask each officer to sign the new shift pattern privately
Talk only to the officers who are not union members
Consult the union early, as agreements require

questions.stem: Which is the most common reason people resist a change at work?
options: Fear of losing something they value, such as skills or status
A wish to make their manager look bad before senior staff
A lack of interest in the work of the organisation as a whole
A belief that every change in the public service must fail

questions.stem: A senior clerk who has run the paper filing system for 20 years openly criticises the new electronic records system. What should the change manager do first?
options: Report the clerk to human resources for disrupting the work
Move the clerk to a unit where the change does not apply
Meet the clerk to hear his concerns and use his skill
Announce at a staff meeting that criticism is not allowed

questions.stem: Why might a change manager choose respected officers from each section to act as "change champions"?
options: They can approve the change budget without the director
Colleagues trust them to share news and pass on concerns
They will do all the training, so no outside help is needed
Their role is to report the colleagues who resist the change

questions.stem: An agency plans to roll out a new online appointment system to 14 parish offices. What is the main advantage of piloting it in two offices first?
options: The other offices will never need any training
The agency can skip consulting the staff union
It removes all of the risk from the full roll-out
Problems can be found and fixed before the full roll-out

questions.stem: Why do change managers plan for some early, visible successes, often called "quick wins"?
options: To let the project finish well before its planned end date
To give the change team something to tell the media
To show the change is working and keep people's support
To reduce the need to measure the final results

questions.stem: Which item belongs in the risk register for a move to a new payroll system at a ministry?
options: Officers may be paid wrongly if old data moves with errors
The project team will meet every Tuesday at 10:00 a.m.
The new system was chosen after a fair tender process
The director has approved the project's terms of reference

questions.stem: An officer believes a planned change to the complaints process will make the public wait longer. What is the most suitable way for her to contribute?
options: Refuse to follow the new process when it starts next month
Give her evidence to the change team through the agreed channel
Post her concerns on social media so that the public knows
Say nothing, since officers must accept every decision made

questions.stem: Which is the best-written objective for a change to the queue system at a passport office?
options: Make the queue system much better for everyone who uses it
Bring in a modern queue system as soon as funds are found
Reduce complaints about the queue to a reasonable level
Cut the average wait from 90 to 45 minutes by June 2027

questions.stem: During the roll-out of a new case management system, how should the project manager track whether the change is on course?
options: Wait for the final evaluation at the end of the second year
Ask the supplier to report on how well its system is going
Check agreed measures against the plan at set points
Rely on officers to send an email if they notice problems

questions.stem: During a restructuring, several officers in a unit show signs of stress and worry about their future. What should their manager do?
options: Check in with them, share what is known and point to support
Tell them that worrying will not change the final decision
Avoid the subject until all the new posts have been filled
Give them extra work so they have less time to think about it

questions.stem: A new procurement system will need officers to use new skills. What should the change manager do before the system goes live?
options: Send each officer a copy of the supplier's full user manual
Train only the supervisors and let them pass it on in time
Wait to see who struggles after go-live, then train them
Find the skill gaps and give hands-on training in good time

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a post-implementation review after a change?
options: To find the officers to blame for any delays
To check results against aims and record lessons
To start planning the next change straight away
To close the project's budget code in the system

questions.stem: Which action best helps to make a new way of working permanent in a public body?
options: Building it into policies, job descriptions and work plans
Sending a reminder email to all staff every six months
Keeping the project team in place for another three years
Holding a launch event with the minister and the media

questions.stem: Moving licence renewals online will cut the cost of each renewal from J$1,200 to J$450. The agency handles 40,000 renewals a year. What is the yearly saving?
A change project costs J$36,000,000 and is expected to save J$12,000,000 a year. How long will the savings take to repay the cost?
options: 2 years
3 years
4 years
12 years

questions.stem: Early in a change, not all decisions have been made. Which message to staff is most helpful?
options: Nothing will change for anyone, so there is no need to worry
We cannot share anything until every detail is decided
Ask your supervisor, who will have heard more than we have
Here is what we know, what we don't, and when we'll update you

questions.stem: Over three years, a ministry changes its whole structure, its culture and the way it serves the public. What type of change is this?
options: Transformational change
Incremental change
Routine change
Temporary change

questions.stem: Which description best fits incremental change?
options: A sudden overhaul of the whole organisation at one time
A change forced on a body by a court or tribunal ruling
Small, steady improvements to existing ways of working
A change that affects only the senior management team

questions.stem: In a change project at a public body, what is the main role of the sponsor, such as the head of the agency?
options: To carry out the day-to-day tasks in the project plan
To train every officer on the new system as it is used
To write the minutes of the project team's meetings
To champion the change and secure its resources

questions.stem: Why does a large change project at a public body usually have a steering committee?
options: To carry out the technical work that the project needs
To give direction, make key decisions and oversee progress
To deal with complaints that the public may make later
To take the place of the agency's board during the change

questions.stem: Halfway through a change project, senior officers keep asking for extra features to be added. What should the project manager do?
options: Accept every request so senior officers stay supportive
Refuse all of the requests without looking at them
Assess each request through the change control process
Add the features quietly and extend the deadline

questions.stem: A change to a new client database means moving the personal data of 50,000 citizens. Which step fits the general purpose of the data protection law?
options: Move only the data needed, securely, and protect it
Copy all the data to officers' laptops so the move is quicker
Keep the old and new databases open to all staff for a year
Ask the supplier to keep a full copy of the data for testing

questions.stem: A director tells all units to book meetings through the new shared online calendar, but she still books her own meetings by phone through her secretary. What is the most likely effect?
options: Staff will use the calendar more because she is so busy
Her own division will adopt the change faster than others
Officers will see no link between her actions and theirs
Officers will see the change as optional and adopt it slowly

questions.stem: The target is for 80% of applications to be made online by year end. At mid-year, 6,300 of 9,000 applications were made online. What percentage is this?
Why should a change manager set up ways for staff to give feedback during the roll-out?
options: Front-line staff often spot problems the plan did not foresee
Feedback means the manager need not make any decisions
It shows the manager which officers are against the change
It removes the need for a formal evaluation at the end

questions.stem: A restructuring cuts the number of supervisor posts in an agency from 12 to 8. Which approach to filling the eight posts is fairest?
options: Keep the eight supervisors the director knows best
Keep the eight who complained least about the change
Use clear, agreed selection criteria applied to all
Let the twelve supervisors decide among themselves

questions.stem: Which response to resistance is most likely to cause problems in the long term?
options: Involving resisters in designing parts of the change
Forcing the change through with threats of discipline
Giving extra training to officers who lack confidence
Explaining the reasons again with clear evidence

questions.stem: Which document sets out the activities, timeline, resources and responsibilities for putting a change into effect?
options: A job description
A risk register
A stakeholder map
A change implementation plan

questions.stem: Which is NOT usually a sign that a change has become embedded?
options: Staff use the new process without being reminded
New staff learn only the new way at induction
Officers keep their old paper forms just in case
Results meet targets for several months in a row

questions.stem: Where should the lessons learned from a change project be kept so they help future projects?
options: In a shared lessons register that future teams can use
In the project manager's personal notebook at home
Only in the minds of the officers who took part
In the final meeting's minutes, filed and closed

questions.stem: A team leader is asked how a proposed new shift system would affect her unit. What should her answer include?
options: Only the views of the officers who like the new system
A general statement that the unit will cope as usual
A list of reasons why the change should be cancelled
Effects on workload, service and staff, with evidence

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Name the psychologist whose three-stage change model uses the stages unfreeze, change and refreeze.
In force field analysis, what are the forces that push for a change called?
What term is used for the figures measured before a change starts, against which later results are compared?
What is the name for running the old and new systems side by side for a period before the old one is switched off?
What term describes rolling out a change in stages, one office or group at a time?
What term describes the uncontrolled growth of a project's aims and tasks after it has started?
Give the six-letter abbreviation for the tool used to scan the political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental drivers of change.
What name is given to a person, from inside or outside the organisation, whose role is to lead and help bring about a change?
Each of the 25 officers in a unit must attend a two-day course on a new system. How many training days is that in total?
A change is expected to cut the average time to process an application from 20 working days to 12. By what percentage will the time fall?
What term is used for the date on which a new system or process first starts to be used for real work?
Which document records the possible problems of a change project, how likely and serious each is, and how each will be managed?
What one word describes the people or groups who affect, or are affected by, a change?
A change project has a budget of J$8,000,000 and has spent J$5,200,000 so far. What percentage of the budget has been spent?
On the change curve, what is usually the first reaction when people hear about a major change?

essays.stem: A government agency in Kingston must move its trade licence applications from paper to an online service within 12 months. You are the change manager. Prepare an outline change plan.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would confirm the aims with the agency head as sponsor, for example 70% of applications online in year one and processing time cut from 20 to 10 working days, and record the baseline figures. I would set up a small steering committee and a project team that includes front-line officers and IT staff. Next I would carry out a stakeholder analysis covering officers, supervisors, the staff union, applicants, business groups and the IT supplier, and a change impact assessment showing how each officer's tasks will change. I would draw up a communication plan with regular briefings, a question channel and updates for the public. The implementation plan would set out tasks, dates and owners: system build and testing, data migration, training, a pilot in one office, then a phased roll-out with a period of parallel running. A risk register would cover data errors, system downtime and resistance. I would track agreed measures monthly, hold a post-implementation review, and build the new process into procedures and job descriptions.
markingPoints: Sets clear, measurable aims with a baseline and a sponsor
Analyses stakeholders and the impact on staff
Includes a communication and consultation plan
Plans training, a pilot and a phased roll-out with risks managed
Monitors, reviews and embeds the change

essays.stem: Compare Lewin's three-stage model with the ADKAR model, and recommend which one a manager should use to guide a restructuring of a parish office.
essays.modelAnswer: Lewin's model sees change in three stages for the organisation: unfreeze, where people see why the old way must go; change, where new ways are introduced; and refreeze, where the new ways are made stable. Its strength is that it is simple and reminds managers not to skip preparing people or embedding the change. Its weakness is that it is very broad, gives little detail on what to do, and treats change as a single event in a world where change is often continuous. ADKAR focuses on the individual: each person needs awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement. Its strength is that it helps a manager find exactly where each officer is stuck, for example someone who understands the change but lacks training. Its weakness is that it says less about structures and systems. For a restructuring of a parish office, which affects people's roles and feelings directly, I would recommend using Lewin's stages to plan the overall phases and ADKAR to check and support each officer. Using both gives a structure for the project and a practical tool for the people side.
markingPoints: Describes Lewin's three stages accurately
Describes the five ADKAR elements accurately
Gives a strength and a weakness of each model
Recognises organisation-level versus individual-level focus
Makes a justified recommendation for the restructuring

essays.stem: Explain the main causes of resistance to change in a public body, and evaluate four ways a manager can respond to it.
essays.modelAnswer: People resist change when they fear losing something they value, such as their job, status, skills or familiar routines. Others resist because they do not understand the reasons, do not trust management after past changes that failed, feel they were not consulted, or genuinely believe the change is flawed. Workload during the change and poor timing also add to resistance. The first response is education and communication: explaining the reasons with evidence works well when resistance comes from lack of information, but takes time. Second, participation: involving officers in designing parts of the change builds ownership and often improves the plan, though it can slow decisions. Third, support: training, coaching and listening help those who are anxious or lack skills, but cost time and money. Fourth, negotiation, for example agreeing changes to shifts with the union, can settle real losses but may set expensive precedents. Forcing change with threats may seem quick but usually damages trust and leads to quiet non-compliance. A good manager treats resistance as information, finds its cause, and chooses the response that fits.
markingPoints: Explains several causes of resistance (fear of loss, lack of understanding, distrust, not consulted)
Evaluates communication and education
Evaluates participation and involvement
Evaluates support and negotiation, noting costs and limits
Warns against coercion and links the response to the cause

essays.stem: Two parish offices of a government agency, in Spanish Town and Old Harbour, are to be merged into one office. Describe the communication plan you would prepare for staff and the public.
essays.modelAnswer: The plan would start with the key messages: why the offices are merging, what will stay the same, what will change, the timeline and where to get help. For staff, the director would announce the merger in person at each office before any public news, so officers do not hear it from outside. Supervisors would then hold team meetings to discuss what it means for each unit, and each affected officer would have a one-to-one meeting. The staff union would be consulted early, as agreements require. I would set up a question channel and publish answers to common questions, with an update every two weeks even when there is little news. For the public, the agency would give at least two months' notice through notices in both offices, its website and social media, local radio and community groups, giving the new address, opening hours and transport routes. Staff would be briefed before the public so they can answer questions. Finally, I would check whether the messages are understood through feedback and adjust the plan.
markingPoints: Sets clear key messages covering why, what, when and support
Tells staff first, face to face, then by unit and individually
Consults the union and provides a two-way question channel
Plans public notice through suitable local channels
Checks understanding and adjusts the plan

essays.stem: Explain how you would carry out a force field analysis for moving a ministry's paper records to an electronic system, and how you would use the results.
essays.modelAnswer: I would bring together a small group, including records officers, IT staff and a supervisor, so the analysis reflects different views. We would write the goal in the middle of a chart: all new records stored electronically by a set date. On one side we would list the driving forces, such as faster searches, less storage space, a government policy on digital services and fewer lost files. On the other side we would list the restraining forces, such as fear of the new system, weak computer skills, the cost of scanning old files and unreliable internet in some offices. We would score each force from 1 (weak) to 5 (strong) and add up each side. If the restraining forces are close to or above the driving forces, the change is at risk. I would use the results to plan actions, focusing on reducing the strongest restraining forces, for example by training, a help desk and better internet, rather than only pushing harder. The chart would also feed the risk register and the communication plan.
markingPoints: Involves a range of people in the analysis
States the goal and lists relevant driving forces
Lists relevant restraining forces
Scores and totals the forces and interprets the result
Uses the results to plan actions, especially reducing restraining forces

essays.stem: Explain how an officer who is not a manager can contribute positively to a change process in a public body.
essays.modelAnswer: An officer can contribute first by understanding the change: reading the briefings, attending meetings and asking questions when something is unclear. Front-line officers know the daily work best, so they can give useful evidence on how a change will affect workload, service to the public and risks, through the agreed channels such as consultation meetings, surveys or their supervisor. If they have concerns, they should raise them early and professionally, with facts and suggested solutions, rather than complaining informally or on social media. Officers can volunteer to help, for example by testing a new system, joining a pilot or acting as a change champion. They should take part in training and practise new skills, and help colleagues who find the change hard. During the roll-out they can report problems quickly so they are fixed. They should also look after their own wellbeing and use the support offered. Finally, once decisions are made, a professional officer follows the new procedures, even if they had doubts, while still giving feedback for improvement.
markingPoints: Seeks to understand the change and asks questions
Gives evidence and raises concerns early through proper channels
Volunteers to help, such as testing, pilots or acting as a champion
Takes part in training and supports colleagues
Follows agreed decisions while continuing to give feedback

essays.stem: A passport office introduced an online appointment system six months ago. The aim was to cut the average wait from 90 to 45 minutes. Describe how you would evaluate whether the change achieved its aims.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start from the aims and the baseline set before the change: an average wait of 90 minutes, with a target of 45. I would collect data on waiting times from the queue system for the last six months and compare it with the baseline, month by month, to see the trend. I would also look at other measures that show whether the change caused new problems, such as the number of missed appointments, complaints, the share of applicants who still walk in without booking, and processing errors. I would ask applicants for feedback through a short survey, including people with less internet access, to check the system is fair to all. I would ask officers how the change affected their workload and what could be improved. I would compare the costs of the change with its benefits. The findings would go into a short report: what was achieved, what was not, the reasons, and recommendations. Lessons would be recorded in a register for future projects, and successful practices built into procedures.
markingPoints: Compares results with the aims and the baseline
Uses several measures, including side effects and complaints
Gathers feedback from the public, including fairness of access, and from staff
Considers costs against benefits
Reports findings, recommendations and lessons learned

essays.stem: A restructuring at a government agency will reduce the number of posts in your division. Explain how you would support staff wellbeing and treat staff fairly during the process.
essays.modelAnswer: Fairness starts with a clear, open process. I would make sure the reasons for the restructuring and the timeline are explained honestly and early, and that the staff union is consulted as agreements and policy require. Selection for the remaining posts must use clear criteria agreed in advance and applied equally to all, with records kept, and the process must follow employment law and public service rules. Staff should know how to appeal. For wellbeing, I would hold one-to-one meetings with each officer to listen to their concerns and explain options such as redeployment, retraining or voluntary separation where offered. I would tell staff about the employee assistance programme or counselling, and watch for signs of stress, referring anyone at risk to professional help. I would try to limit uncertainty by giving regular updates, even when there is little news. Workloads would be reviewed so staff are not overloaded during the change. Finally, I would remember those who stay: they may feel guilt or worry, so they also need support and a clear picture of the new structure.
markingPoints: Explains reasons and timeline honestly and consults the union
Uses clear, agreed selection criteria and follows law and rules, with a right of appeal
Holds one-to-one meetings and explains options
Points staff to professional support and watches for stress
Gives regular updates, manages workload and supports those who stay

essays.stem: Explain why many changes in organisations fail to last, and describe how a manager can embed a change so that it becomes the normal way of working.
essays.modelAnswer: Many changes fail to last because attention moves on once the launch is over. The project team is disbanded, leaders stop talking about the change, and old habits return, especially under pressure. Sometimes the new way was never fully built into the systems people use, so old forms and shortcuts remain. Changes also fade when staff were not convinced of the benefits, when training was too short, or when performance measures still reward the old behaviour. To embed a change, the manager should write the new way into policies, procedures, job descriptions and induction, and remove the old forms and systems where possible. Performance plans and targets should reflect the new way, and success should be measured and shared so people see the benefits. Leaders must keep using and talking about the change themselves. Refresher training and a named person to answer questions help in the first months. The manager should check results for several months after go-live and act quickly if people slip back.
markingPoints: Explains why changes fade (attention moves on, old systems remain, weak buy-in)
Builds the change into policies, procedures and induction
Removes the old ways and aligns measures and targets
Leaders model the change and share results
Gives ongoing support and monitors for slipping back

essays.stem: A ministry must choose between switching all 13 parish offices to a new payroll system on one day ("big bang") or switching a few offices at a time (phased). Compare the two approaches and recommend one, with reasons.
essays.modelAnswer: A big bang switch-over means every office starts the new payroll system on the same day. Its advantages are that it is quicker, avoids running two systems for months and gives everyone the same date. Its main disadvantage is risk: if the system or the data has problems, every officer in the ministry could be paid late or wrongly at the same time, and the support team may be overwhelmed. A phased approach moves a few offices at a time. It lowers the risk, because problems found in the first offices can be fixed before the rest move, and trainers and support staff can focus on a few offices at once. Its disadvantages are that it takes longer, costs more, and for a time two systems must be run and reconciled. Because payroll errors directly harm staff and would damage trust in the change, I would recommend the phased approach, beginning with a pilot of two offices and a period of parallel running, with clear go or no-go checks before each new phase.
markingPoints: Explains the big bang approach with an advantage and a disadvantage
Explains the phased approach with an advantage and a disadvantage
Considers the special risk of payroll errors to staff
Makes a clear recommendation
Justifies it and adds safeguards such as a pilot, parallel running or checkpoints

practical1.title: Prepare a change management plan for a public body
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up case: a government agency with parish offices that must replace paper application files with an online system within one year. The pack includes the agency's aims, staff numbers, a short staff survey and the budget. As a group, prepare a change management plan for the agency head. Each member has a named role: stakeholder analyst (lists the stakeholders and draws a power-interest grid with an action for each group); change analyst (leads a force field analysis with the group, scores the forces, and writes a short impact assessment of how officers' work will change); communication planner (writes a communication plan with key messages, audiences, channels, timing and a question channel); implementation planner (draws a timeline or Gantt chart showing training, pilot and phased roll-out, and a risk register with at least five risks); and presenter (presents the plan to the assessor, acting as agency head, in 10 minutes). In a group of four, the implementation planner also presents. Every member must answer at least one question from the assessor.
materials: Computers with word processing, spreadsheet and presentation software
Flipchart paper, sticky notes and markers
Templates for a power-interest grid, risk register and communication plan
photos: The power-interest grid with an action for each stakeholder group
The force field analysis chart with scores and totals
The timeline or Gantt chart and the risk register
The group presenting the plan to the assessor
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the plan
Stakeholders are placed sensibly on the grid with suitable actions
Force field scores are added correctly and used to plan actions
Communication plan tells staff first, uses several channels and allows questions
Timeline includes training, a pilot and a phased roll-out in a sensible order
Risk register gives likelihood, impact and a response for each risk
Explained and defended the plan when questioned
safety: Treat the case pack and survey results as confidential; return all printouts to the assessor
Use made-up names and agencies only; do not discuss real colleagues or real restructurings
Respect each other's ideas and share the workload fairly
Take a short screen break each hour

practical2.title: Role-play a change briefing and a staff consultation meeting
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up case: a parish office of a public body will move to a new shift pattern and a new queue system in three months. Part A (about 1 hour): plan and hold a 15-minute briefing to staff. One member plays the director, who announces the change; the other members play officers, each with a role card from the assessor (for example an anxious officer, a long-serving supervisor who opposes the change, and a union delegate). Part B (about 1 hour): hold a 20-minute consultation meeting, chaired by a different member as the unit manager, to hear concerns and agree next steps. One member is note-taker in each part and writes the notes and an action log. Rotate roles so every member speaks as a manager or director at least once. Part C (about 30 minutes): as a group, write a one-page "questions and answers" sheet for staff, based on the concerns raised, and a short summary of the feedback for the change team. Each member writes at least two of the answers.
materials: Case card and role cards from the assessor
A room set up for a staff briefing, with a flipchart
Computer and printer, or paper and pens
photos: The director's briefing notes or slides
The briefing or consultation meeting in progress (faces only if all agree)
The meeting notes and the action log
The finished questions and answers sheet
The feedback summary for the change team
checklist: Explained the reasons for the change, what will and will not change, and the timeline
Listened to concerns and responded calmly and honestly, without making promises that cannot be kept
Treated the union delegate's points with respect and agreed how consultation will continue
Recorded accurate notes and clear actions with owners and dates
Wrote clear, accurate answers for the questions and answers sheet
Summarised the feedback fairly for the change team
safety: Use only the made-up case; do not discuss real staff matters or real colleagues
